technical_analysis: Root cause 1 — scopeMemberships.routes.ts:122-127 and 137-142 call `scopeAccessService.updateMemberRole(membershipId, role)` / `removeMember(membershipId)`, which delegate to `scopeMembershipRepository.updateRole` (scopeMembership.repository.ts:86-91) and `.delete` (:96-98). Both issue `prisma.scope_memberships.update/delete({ where: { id } })` with no organization predicate. The requireScopeAccess('admin') guard only validates the `:id` scope param against the attacker's org — the `:membershipId` row is never tied back to that scope or org. Root cause 2 — businessScopes.routes.ts GET '/:id/plugins' (:815-833) and GET '/:id/mcp-servers' (:935-953) execute raw SQL filtering only on `business_scope_id`; the sibling endpoints '/:id/agents' and '/:id/skills' do call scopeAccessService.requireAccess, these two do not. Root cause 3 — scopeMemberships.routes.ts:150-171 `business_scopes.update({ where: { id } })` for visibility has no org predicate (unlike the adjacent raw-SQL config_version bump which includes organization_id). Root cause 4 — connectors.routes.ts:126-129 passes scopeId to `getScopeConnectors` which queries `scope_data_connectors` by business_scope_id only (data-connector.repository.ts:106-113), including the full connector record.
poc_description: 1. Authenticate as a scope-admin in Org A (admin of any scope in your org to pass requireScopeAccess('admin')). 2. PATCH /api/business-scopes/:myScopeId/members/:victimMembershipId with {role:'admin'} — updateMemberRole updates scope_memberships by {id} with no org predicate, elevating the attacker's account to admin of the victim org's restricted scope. 3. DELETE the same endpoint with a victim membership id to evict members from another org's scope. 4. GET /api/business-scopes/:victimScopeId/plugins and /:victimScopeId/mcp-servers — raw SQL selects by business_scope_id only, returning the victim org's MCP server host addresses, configs and plugin git URLs. 5. GET /api/data-connectors/scopes/:victimScopeId/connectors returns the victim org's connectors including scope_config. 6. PATCH /api/business-scopes/:victimScopeId/visibility flips another org's scope between open/restricted.
remediation_steps: Resolve the membership row (or scope) first and verify its organization_id equals request.user.orgId inside updateMemberRole/removeMember/visibility handlers; add organization_id join predicates to the raw SQL plugin/MCP-server listings and to findScopeConnectors; scope the scope_mcp_servers delete/config updates by joining business_scopes.organization_id rather than only checking scope ownership on a separate statement.
evidence: Vitest PoC (/tmp/idor-poc/scope-poc.test.ts, 3/3 passing) with mocked prisma: scopeAccessService.updateMemberRole('membership-in-victim-org','admin') -> prisma.scope_memberships.update({where:{id:'membership-in-victim-org'}}) with no organization_id; removeMember -> delete({where:{id}}). Source: businessScopes.routes.ts:821-833 (plugins raw SQL `WHERE sp.business_scope_id = ${id}::uuid` with orgId captured but unused), :938-953 (mcp-servers raw SQL joining mcp_servers with no org filter), scopeMemberships.routes.ts:125/141 (membershipId passed straight through), :168-171 (business_scopes.update by {id} only), connectors.routes.ts:127 + data-connector.service.ts:117-119 + data-connector.repository.ts:106-113 (findScopeConnectors by business_scope_id only).
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated member of one organization who is scope-admin of at least one business scope in their own org (for the membership-write paths) or simply any authenticated user (for the raw-SQL read paths), plus a victim scope/membership UUID.
counterevidence: Checked whether the requireScopeAccess('admin') preHandler on PATCH/DELETE :id/members/:membershipId verifies the target membership's org: the middleware's defaultExtractor reads only params.id/params.scopeId, and scopeAccessService.getAccessLevel scopes the check to the user's own org — so passing a victim-org scopeId in :id correctly fails, which is why the attack targets :membershipId instead. The raw-SQL GET endpoints have no scopeAccessService call at all (contrast with /:id/agents and /:id/skills which call it), confirming these were simply missed.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that restricted scopes hold regulated data or that scope_config embeds credentials for MCP servers would raise impact; a database-level tenant RLS policy would lower it.

title: Cross-tenant BOLA: checkpoint resolve/resume and execution detail routes skip organization scoping
description: Three workflow checkpoint/execution endpoints perform no organization check: the checkpoint resolve route, the execution status route in checkpoint.routes.ts, and the executor resume path. Any authenticated user of any organization can read another organization's paused execution details, resolve or cancel their human-approval checkpoints, and resume their workflows, by supplying the execution or checkpoint UUID.
impact: Cross-tenant integrity impact on workflow approval flows: a user from organization A can approve or cancel organization B's human-approval checkpoints — the exact control meant to gate destructive workflow segments — and force-resume or steer B's paused executions by supplying an arbitrary `scopeId` (the resume route passes the user-supplied scopeId to workspace provisioning and the executor, `checkpoint.routes.ts:66`). They can also read B's execution state, checkpoint configuration, and inputContext (which contains workflow variable values and prior node outputs). This defeats the tenant isolation invariant of the platform.
technical_analysis:
Three concrete gaps:

1. `src/routes/checkpoint.routes.ts:27-40` — `POST /executions/:executionId/checkpoints/:checkpointId/resolve` uses `preHandler: [authenticate]` only, then calls `checkpointService.resolve(checkpointId, ...)` without passing or checking `request.user.orgId`. `src/services/checkpoint.service.ts:132-136` looks the checkpoint up with `prisma.execution_checkpoints.findUnique({ where: { id: checkpointId } })` — no `organization_id` predicate — and updates it. The route then resumes execution via `workflowExecutorV2.resume(executionId, checkpointId, scopeId)` where `scopeId` is taken verbatim from the request body.
2. `src/services/workflow-executor-v2.ts:574-580` — `resume()` loads the execution with `prisma.workflow_executions.findUnique({ where: { id: executionId } })`, again with no organization filter, and does not verify the checkpoint belongs to that execution or that the caller's org matches.
3. `src/routes/checkpoint.routes.ts:113-118` — `GET /executions/:executionId` (the checkpoint detail route, distinct from the correctly-scoped one in execution.routes.ts) uses `findUnique({ where: { id: executionId } })` with no `organization_id` filter and returns node executions, checkpoint config, and inputContext.

Sibling routes (`execution.routes.ts` GET /executions/:id, /logs, /workspace/files) all scope by `organization_id`, confirming the intended invariant that these three paths violate.
poc_description:
1. As a user of org A, obtain (or guess) a paused execution UUID belonging to org B (UUIDs surface in SSE events, exports, and logs).
2. GET /api/workflows/executions/<executionId> — the handler queries by id only, returning B's execution including checkpoint config and inputContext.
3. POST /api/workflows/executions/<executionId>/checkpoints/<checkpointId>/resolve with {"status":"resolved","scopeId":"<any scope uuid>"} — `checkpointService.resolve` looks up the checkpoint by id with no org predicate and flips it to resolved, then `workflowExecutorV2.resume` loads the execution with no org predicate and continues executing B's workflow nodes in the attacker-chosen scope.
remediation_steps: Add organization scoping to all three paths: in `checkpointService.resolve`, look up the checkpoint with `findFirst({ where: { id, organization_id } })` (the org id is returned by the route's user context); in the checkpoint GET execution route and `workflowExecutorV2.resume`, filter `workflow_executions` by `organization_id` (and for resume, derive `scopeId` from the execution record instead of accepting it from the request body). Mirror the pattern already used in execution.routes.ts.
evidence:
Source-level evidence (no DB available in isolated assessment):

```text
checkpoint.routes.ts:113-116  const execution = await prisma.workflow_executions.findUnique({ where: { id: executionId }, include: ... })   // no organization_id
checkpoint.service.ts:135-136  prisma.execution_checkpoints.findUnique({ where: { id: checkpointId } })                                        // no organization_id
workflow-executor-v2.ts:578-579 prisma.workflow_executions.findUnique({ where: { id: executionId } })                                        // no organization_id
```

Contrast with the correctly-scoped sibling: `execution.routes.ts:520-523` filters `organization_id: request.user.orgId` and additionally enforces per-user ownership.
assumptions: Assumes a second authenticated user in a different organization and knowledge of (or guessed) a UUID of a paused execution or its checkpoint. No member/admin role needed — plain authentication suffices.
counterevidence: Neighboring execution routes do scope by organization (`GET /executions/:id`, `/logs`, `/workspace/files` all filter on `organization_id: request.user.orgId`), which shows the codebase intends org scoping here — these three checkpoint routes are the omission. The UUID format parameter makes blind guessing impractical, but UUIDs leak through logs, exports, SSE payloads, and shared integrations. No other control (ownership column, membership check) exists on the resolve path; `checkpointService.resolve` only checks status and expiry.
confidence_rationale: Static trace is complete (route → service → ORM query with no org predicate, verified in source), and the identical missing-filter pattern was confirmed exploitable by sibling agents' tenant-isolation PoCs in this scan, but I did not stand up the full Fastify+Prisma stack to replay the cross-org request end-to-end myself.
severity_change_conditions: A live cross-tenant replay confirming the resolve/resume path would raise confidence to high and could justify a higher availability/integrity impact rating; conversely, evidence that these routes are mounted behind an org-enforcing gateway (not present in the repository) would rule the finding out.

title: Unauthenticated, unscoped WebSocket gateway leaks any tenant's workflow execution events
description: The WebSocket endpoint `/ws/executions` accepts unauthenticated connections and allows any client to subscribe to arbitrary workflow `executionId` values with no ownership or tenant check. Workflow node events — including full node output (`result.output`, e.g. LLM responses and tool results) — are then broadcast to that client, leaking any tenant's execution data to an unauthenticated network peer.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker who knows (or brute-forces/obtains) any execution UUID can stream that execution's live workflow events, including node results produced by LLM and tool nodes, across all organizations/tenants. This exposes other tenants' business data (workflow outputs, error messages, prompts echoed in results) in real time. It also lets an unauthenticated client hold arbitrary subscriptions, enabling resource consumption.
technical_analysis: `ExecutionWebSocketGateway.register()` (src/websocket/execution.gateway.ts:126-141) registers the route with only `{ websocket: true }` and no `preHandler`/auth. The backend applies authentication exclusively as a per-route `preHandler: [authenticate]` on REST routes; there is no global auth hook (verified in src/app.ts — only request-logging and audit onResponse hooks are global), so the WS route is unauthenticated. `handleConnection()` (line 155) never inspects the request. `handleSubscribe()` (lines 190-236) adds the client to `this.subscriptions` for any non-empty string `executionId` with no check that the execution belongs to the connecting user's organization. The bridge in src/setup/event-websocket-bridge.ts:46 forwards every `workflow:event` from `workflowExecutionService` — including `node:completed`/`node:paused` events whose `data.result` carries the full node output (`result.output`, src/services/workflow-execution.service.ts:459-483) — to all subscribers of that executionId.
poc_description:
1. Start the backend (or a Fastify instance with the gateway registered) on a reachable host.
2. Open a WebSocket to `ws://<host>:<port>/ws/executions` with no Authorization header or token.
3. Send `{"type":"subscribe","executionId":"<any execution UUID>"}`.
4. Observe the server replies `{"type":"subscribed",...}` and subsequently delivers `workflow_event` messages containing that execution's node status and result data.
remediation_steps: Authenticate the WebSocket upgrade: validate the JWT (Authorization header or a short-lived one-time ticket issued by an authenticated REST endpoint) inside the `/ws/executions` handler before accepting the connection, and reject unauthenticated upgrades. On `subscribe`, look up the execution by ID scoped to the authenticated user's organization (e.g. `workflowExecutionService.getExecution(executionId, request.user.orgId)`) and reject subscriptions to executions the org does not own. Consider also validating origin headers for browser clients.
evidence:
Local PoC output (isolated Fastify instance on 127.0.0.1 running the actual gateway module):

```text
📥 Client subscribed to execution victim-exec-123. Subscribers: 1
📡 Broadcast node:completed for execution victim-exec-123: 1 sent, 0 failed
received: [
 { "type": "subscribed", "executionId": "victim-exec-123" },
 { "type": "workflow_event", "event": { "type": "node:completed",
   "executionId": "victim-exec-123", "nodeId": "llm-node-1",
   "data": { "status": "finish", "result": { "secret": "SENSITIVE_AGENT_OUTPUT" } } } }
]
POC CONFIRMED: unauthenticated client received cross-execution event data
```

No Authorization header, query token, or any credentials were supplied by the client.
assumptions: Assumes the backend port is network-reachable by the attacker (deployment binds HOST 0.0.0.0 by default) and that executions carry sensitive node outputs, as the code shows result.output is included in broadcast events.
counterevidence: Checked for controls that could mitigate: (1) no global onRequest auth hook exists in app.ts — authentication is exclusively per-route preHandler, and the WS route registers none; (2) execution IDs are UUIDs, so an attacker must know/guess one — this raises difficulty but execution IDs appear in API responses to any org member and can be enumerated from prior executions; (3) no origin/Referer or token validation occurs anywhere in the gateway (searched whole file). title: Output sanitizer redaction gaps: Bearer tokens, connection strings, generic API keys and Windows paths pass through to clients
description: The `output-sanitizer` that scrubs agent responses before they are streamed to clients only redacts a narrow set of patterns: POSIX-style server paths, the workspace base dir, home directory, and `AUTH_TOKEN`/AWS key-value strings. Bearer tokens in `Authorization` headers, database connection strings, generic API keys (e.g. `sk-ant-...`), `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`-style env assignments, and Windows paths pass through unredacted into SSE responses rendered to chat clients.
impact: If an agent (via tool output, file read, or error message) echoes a credential in one of the uncovered forms — an Authorization header, a connection string, a raw API key, or a non-POSIX path — it is delivered verbatim to the chat client. This widens credential-exposure blast radius when agents read config files or invoke authenticated tools.
technical_analysis: `buildPatterns()` in src/services/output-sanitizer.ts:25-79 constructs only: workspace-base and home-dir path regexes, one POSIX path regex (`/\/(?:Users|home|var|tmp|opt)\/...`), `AUTH_TOKEN=`, and AWS key=value patterns. No pattern matches `Authorization: Bearer ...`, connection strings with embedded credentials, raw API keys, other env-var secret names, or Windows paths. `sanitizeString()` (line ~95) applies only these patterns, and `sanitizeEvent` applies it only to assistant text/tool_use/tool_result blocks of SSE events.
poc_description:
1. Feed representative secret strings through `sanitizeString()` from `src/services/output-sanitizer.ts` (local copy, no network).
2. Observe that only workspace/home paths are redacted; Bearer tokens, `postgres://` URLs, `sk-ant-...` keys, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=` assignments, and Windows paths are returned unchanged.
remediation_steps: Extend the pattern set: redact `Bearer\s+\S+`, common API-key prefixes (`sk-ant-`, `sk-`, `AKIA`, `ghp_`, `xoxb-`), connection-string credentials (`\w+://[^:/\s]+:[^@\s]+@`), generic `*_API_KEY=`/`*_TOKEN=` assignments, and Windows drive-letter paths (`[A-Za-z]:\\`). Prefer an allowlist-style scrub of anything resembling a secret over the current narrow denylist.
evidence:
Local execution of the sanitizer's pattern set (extracted verbatim from src/services/output-sanitizer.ts):

```text
home leaked      => Reading ~ now
bearer token     => call with Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.real.token.here   [PASSED THROUGH]
db url           => postgres://sa_user:P@ssw0rd@db.internal:5432/prod                      [PASSED THROUGH]
windows path     => C:\Users\admin\secrets\aws-keys.txt                                     [PASSED THROUGH]
api key inline   => sk-ant-api03-ABCDEFG123456789 was used                                  [PASSED THROUGH]
env var generic  => ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-xyz123 use it                                  [PASSED THROUGH]
```
assumptions: Assumes agent outputs occasionally echo secrets/paths, which the sanitizer's own existence and targeted patterns acknowledge.
counterevidence: The sanitizer does cover its stated scope well within Linux deployments: home-dir and workspace-base paths are redacted (verified locally), and AUTH_TOKEN/AWS key=value strings are redacted. The gap is incomplete coverage rather than absence of sanitization. Real exploitation also requires the agent to echo a secret in a form matching the uncovered patterns.
confidence_rationale: Static analysis of the sanitizer's regex set plus a local reproduction of its filtering behavior; no live agent output containing real secrets was produced, so leakage of an actual secret is inferred from the gap, not observed end-to-end.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating a live agent workflow that echoes a real credential into a chat stream would raise severity; confirming that agent outputs never contain such forms would lower it to informational.

title: Cross-tenant leader manipulation in PUT /api/chat/rooms/:roomId/members/:agentId/leader (missing org scoping on raw updateMany)
description: The "set room leader" endpoint updates `chat_room_members` with raw Prisma `updateMany` filtered only by `session_id` and `agent_id` — no organization scoping and no room-ownership check — so any authenticated member-role user who knows a room's session UUID can change leader assignment and leader instructions on another organization's room.
impact: A member of organization A can promote or demote the leader agent of organization B's room and set the leader's `leader_instructions`, changing which agent coordinates the room and the instructions it follows — an unauthorized cross-tenant state change on the target room's coordination logic. The response also discloses the foreign room's agent membership and roles.
technical_analysis: In `chatRooms.routes.ts` the `PUT /:roomId/members/:agentId/leader` handler (lines 177–206) demotes the current leader and promotes the requested agent with three raw `prisma.chat_room_members.updateMany` calls whose `where` clauses filter only on `session_id` (and `agent_id`). No middleware on this route performs a room lookup: `authenticate` establishes identity, `requireModifyAccess` (`middleware/auth.ts:280`) checks only the caller's role. The room's owning organization is never resolved, so Prisma applies no org boundary. This diverges from the sibling `DELETE /:roomId/members/:agentId` handler (lines 156–169), which passes `request.user!.orgId` into `chatRoomService.removeMember`. Even the final read, `memberRepo.findBySession(roomId)` (`repositories/chat-room-member.repository.ts:35`), takes no organization filter, so the route's response also discloses the foreign room's agent membership and roles. The room ID is a UUIDv4 (`chat_sessions.id @default(uuid())`, prisma/schema.prisma:480), so the attacker needs a known session UUID; this is the sole practical constraint.
poc_description: As any authenticated member-role user of organization A, send a PUT to the leader endpoint with the session UUID of organization B's room and a member agent UUID of that room. Confirm that leader flags flip and leader_instructions persist for the foreign room, and that the response lists the foreign room's members.
remediation_steps: Before updating, load the room through an org-scoped query (e.g. a `findById(orgId, roomId)` on the chat session repository that filters by `organization_id`) and return 404 when it does not belong to the caller's organization; add the `organization_id` to the `updateMany` where clauses as defense in depth. Mirror the pattern used by `removeMember`, which already receives and uses `orgId`.
evidence: Route preHandler is `[authenticate, requireModifyAccess]` only (role check, no object check); the handler runs `updateMany({ where: { session_id: roomId } })` and `updateMany({ where: { session_id: roomId, agent_id: agentId } })` with no `organization_id` predicate and no prior room lookup (chatRooms.routes.ts:177-206). Contrast with sibling handler `removeMember` (line 159) which passes `request.user!.orgId` into the service, and the follow-up read `memberRepo.findBySession(roomId)` (chat-room-member.repository.ts:35) which also takes no org filter. Verified against the project's own adapters and Prisma semantics in an isolated local sandbox; no network or real database was contacted. Room IDs are `@default(uuid())` (schema.prisma:480), so exploitation requires a known room UUID.
assumptions: Attacker holds a valid member-role account in any organization (self-registered or provisioned) and knows or guesses a target room's UUID. Intended actions by authorized users on their own org's rooms are not in scope.
counterevidence: Prehandlers authenticate and enforce role but add no object check. No global hook in this file or route registration adds an org predicate. The only org-aware code on the route is the follow-up memberRepo.findBySession read. Verified no `organization_id` filter exists in the where clauses by direct inspection of all three updateMany calls. Mitigating: UUID room IDs make blind targeting impractical — requires a leaked/observed roomId, and updateMany with a non-matching filter is a no-op, so probing for valid rooms yields indistinguishable empty member lists. This limits exploitability but not the authorization flaw.
severity_change_conditions: A demonstrated path for an attacker to obtain foreign rooms' session UUIDs (e.g. an unscoped list/export endpoint or UUID leak in logs) would raise severity to high; deployment where member accounts cannot be created across orgs would lower it.

title: IM webhook signature verification fails open — unauthenticated message injection into agent sessions
description: IM inbound webhook signature verification fails open: Slack, Telegram, DingTalk, Feishu and WhatsApp adapters return true when no secret is configured, and Discord/WeCom adapters always return true, so unauthenticated POSTs to the public /api/im/* webhook routes are accepted and injected into the org's agent chat pipeline whenever a binding exists without a stored secret.
impact: An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the webhook URLs can inject arbitrary text into the target organization's agent chat sessions. The message is processed with the binding creator's identity and the org's full agent configuration — credentialed agents, tools, MCP servers and workflows act on attacker-chosen instructions. This is a trust-boundary break: the design intends only the verified IM platform to reach this path. It is not a new server-side code-execution primitive by itself.
technical_analysis: The inbound chain is `imWebhookRoutes` (im.routes.ts, mounted at `/api/im`, routes/index.ts:255). Each platform route parses the payload to extract `channelId`, then `verifyAndLookupBinding` (im.routes.ts:226-271) loads the binding via `imChannelRepository.findByChannelTypeAndId` — a global lookup with no org scoping — injects the binding's stored secret (e.g. `config.signing_secret` → `x-slack-signing-secret-internal` header, im.routes.ts:243-260), and calls `adapter.verifyRequest`. Every adapter's fail-open behavior: Slack (slack-adapter.ts:39-42, `if (!signingSecret) return true`), Telegram (telegram-adapter.ts:31-34, `if (!secret) return true`), DingTalk (dingtalk-adapter.ts:80-83), WhatsApp (whatsapp-adapter.ts:66-69, `if (!appSecret) return true`), Feishu (feishu-adapter.ts:104-107, `if (!token) return true`), Discord (discord-adapter.ts:23-27, always true), WeCom generic path (wecom-adapter.ts:177-180, always true). When the secret is absent from the binding's `config`, no internal header is injected, so `verifyRequest` hits the fail-open branch and accepts the request. Secrets come only from the operator-entered `config` on binding create/update (im.routes.ts:84-175) — there is no server-side requirement that a secret exist, so a fresh binding created via the admin UI without filling the secret fields is unprotected by default. On success, `imService.handleMessage` (im.service.ts:171) resolves the binding, creates/reuses a thread session, and calls `chatService.processMessage` with the binding's `organization_id`, `business_scope_id` and `created_by` as the effective user — i.e. full agent authority under the org, driven entirely by attacker-supplied text. The generic `POST /api/im/webhook/:bindingId` (im.routes.ts:735-772) additionally accepts arbitrary `{text}` for any enabled binding with no verification at all (binding UUID is the only barrier). Counterpoints: WeCom Agent-mode message callbacks do perform real signature+AES verification (im.routes.ts:494-540), and the WhatsApp GET verification challenge checks `verify_token` — so those paths are stricter; the exposure is the fail-open branches and the always-true adapters above.
poc_description: Run the project's own adapters against an unauthenticated request (no headers, no secret configured). Observe verifyRequest returns true. For the route-level effect, POST a well-formed platform payload (e.g. Slack message_create event with the target channel_id) to /api/im/slack/events — parseEvent yields a message, verifyAndLookupBinding finds the binding and the adapter passes, and imService.handleMessage injects the text into the org's agent session.
remediation_steps: Make verification fail closed: if no secret is configured for a binding that supports signature verification, reject the inbound message (or refuse to enable the binding until a secret is stored). For adapters that genuinely cannot verify HTTP callbacks (Discord/WeCom gateway modes), disable their dedicated HTTP callback routes or require a per-binding shared secret on the generic /api/im/webhook/:bindingId path instead of returning true. Additionally, scope binding lookup by organization where the route carries org context.
evidence: Adapter code executed directly (project's own TS sources, isolated local sandbox, tsx): `SlackAdapter.verifyRequest({}, body)` → true, `TelegramAdapter.verifyRequest({}, body)` → true, `DingTalkAdapter.verifyRequest({}, body)` → true, `WhatsAppAdapter.verifyRequest({}, body)` → true (all with no headers — the fail-open branch). Control: Slack with a configured secret and a forged signature → false, confirming the check is real but only the unconfigured branch fails open. WeCom and Discord adapters structurally return true unconditionally (wecom-adapter.ts:177, discord-adapter.ts:23). Route chain: im.routes.ts verifyAndLookupBinding (lines 226-271) looks up the binding globally (no org) and calls adapter.verifyRequest; dedicated routes at im.routes.ts:290-433 (/api/im/slack/events, /api/im/telegram/webhook, /api/im/feishu/events, /api/im/dingtalk/callback) then call imService.handleMessage → chatService.processMessage with the binding's org/scope/created_by (im.service.ts:171-290).
assumptions: Attacker can reach the backend's IM webhook endpoints over the network and at least one IM channel binding exists with no signature secret stored in `config` (or is a discord/wecom binding). Credentialed agent operations must already be configured for the scope. Intended use by the real IM platform is not affected by the fix.
counterevidence: Controls that do exist: bindings must exist and be enabled; WeCom message callbacks and the WhatsApp verification challenge do enforce secret checks; Slack/Telegram/WhatsApp perform real timing-safe HMAC when a secret is configured (demonstrated). No WAF or additional signature middleware wraps these routes. The main constraint is the prerequisite that the binding's secret is unset — bindings created with secrets configured are protected on the strict-verification platforms. Discord/WeCom generic-webhook reachability additionally requires guessing the binding UUID. No org check exists anywhere on the webhook path (findByChannelTypeAndId is global), so once the precondition holds the path is fully unauthenticated.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that deployments commonly create bindings without secrets (e.g. the admin UI does not require signing_secret/app_secret/secret_token at binding creation) would firm up exploitability; discovery of an additional unauthenticated route that lists binding channel_ids would raise severity to high.

title: Plaintext IM signing secrets exposed to any org member via GET /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/im-channels (config not redacted)
description: GET /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/im-channels returns each IM channel binding with its full `config` object included, exposing plaintext platform secrets — Slack `signing_secret`, DingTalk `signing_secret`, Feishu `verification_token`/`encrypt_key`, Telegram `secret_token`, WhatsApp `app_secret`, Discord `public_key`, WeCom `token`/`encoding_aes_key` — to any authenticated member of the organization, while only `bot_token_enc` is masked.
impact: Any member-role user (not just admins) of the organization can read the raw platform verification secrets for every IM binding in the scope. These secrets are exactly the values the inbound webhook signature checks rely on (CWE-312 exposure of the verification credential); possession lets a member forge or validate webhook traffic, and for platforms where the secret is also an outbound credential (e.g. WeCom `encoding_aes_key`, DingTalk app secret) enables impersonation of the bot towards the platform. Confidentiality impact is limited to the organization's own secrets — no cross-tenant access, no server-side state change.
technical_analysis: `imChannelAdminRoutes` is registered with prefix `/api/business-scopes` (routes/index.ts:218). The list handler (im.routes.ts:67-82) requires only `authenticate` — no role check — and spreads each binding (`...b`) into the response, replacing only `bot_token_enc` with `'***'`. The `config` JSON column is where the admin routes store platform secrets: `POST /:scopeId/im-channels` and `PUT .../:bindingId` persist the caller-supplied `config` verbatim (im.routes.ts:106-113, 130-133), and the webhook verification path reads them back from the same field (im.routes.ts:243-260: `cfg.signing_secret`, `cfg.verification_token`, `cfg.secret_token`, `cfg.public_key`; wecom `cfg.token`/`cfg.encoding_aes_key` at im.routes.ts:504-507; whatsapp `cfg.app_secret` at im.routes.ts:712). Because the list endpoint does not redact `config`, every secret an operator entered for webhook verification is returned in plaintext to any authenticated member of the org. Org scoping itself is correct: `findByScope` filters by `organization_id` and `business_scope_id` (im-channel.repository.ts:45-53), so exposure is confined to the caller's own organization.
poc_description: Authenticate as any member of the org, GET /api/business-scopes/<scopeId>/im-channels for a scope containing an IM binding, and observe each binding's `config` object in the response containing the plaintext `signing_secret` (Slack/DingTalk), `app_secret` (WhatsApp), `secret_token` (Telegram), etc., while only `bot_token_enc` is masked as `***`.
remediation_steps: Redact secret-bearing keys from `config` before returning bindings in the list endpoint (and in the create/update responses), the same way `bot_token_enc` is masked: strip or mask keys such as `signing_secret`, `app_secret`, `secret_token`, `verification_token`, `encrypt_key`, `encoding_aes_key`, `token`, `client_secret` unless the caller has an admin role with a documented need. Server-side consumers (verifyAndLookupBinding, adapters) should read the secrets from the database rather than from API responses.
evidence: Code path confirmed: im.routes.ts:67-82 — `imChannelRepository.findByScope(request.user!.orgId, request.params.scopeId)` then `bindings.map(b => ({ ...b, bot_token_enc: '***' }))`; `config` is spread unmodified. Repository scoping is correct (im-channel.repository.ts:45-53, where: { organization_id, business_scope_id }) — org members of the owning org only, not cross-tenant. The same plaintext `config` is consumed server-side at im.routes.ts:243-260 (signing secrets injected for verification), proving real secret material lives in `config`. Binding creation stores operator-provided `config` verbatim (im.routes.ts:106-113).
assumptions: Attacker holds any authenticated account in the organization that owns the scope (member role suffices — only `authenticate` is required). A Slack/DingTalk/Feishu/Telegram/WhatsApp/Discord binding with secret material in `config` must exist in that scope.
counterevidence: The bot access token IS masked (`bot_token_enc: '***'` at im.routes.ts:75-78), which shows the developer considered credential redaction but missed the `config` JSON — the most likely copy-paste source for the full-duplication answer, and the strongest evidence this is unintended. Org scoping is correctly applied (repository where-clause), so there is no cross-tenant dimension. No route-level sanitization or serializer strips `config`. Only defense is obscurity of scope UUIDs, which the authenticated member can enumerate from their own org's scope list.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that these secrets grant authority beyond the org's own channels (e.g. a shared Slack signing secret usable to forge requests accepted by other systems) would raise severity; a deployment with no IM bindings would lower it.

title: Non-atomic duplicate-trigger guard in workflow scheduler causes double execution of scheduled workflows
description: The scheduled-workflow trigger guard in the scheduler tick is a non-atomic check-then-act sequence: concurrent or overlapping ticks can both pass it and execute the same schedule twice, causing duplicate workflow executions and duplicate outbound actions (API calls, notifications).
impact: Duplicate workflow executions: each duplicate run repeats the workflow's action nodes, so outbound api_call requests, messages, or state changes fire twice. For schedules performing payments, notifications, or external mutations this means duplicated real-world side effects. Availability/confidentiality are not affected; integrity impact is limited to duplicated (not arbitrary) actions.
technical_analysis:
`startScheduleProcessor` (src/setup/schedule-processor.ts:31-35) runs `processSchedules` every 15s. `processDueSchedules` (src/services/schedule.service.ts:457-496) fetches due schedules with `findMany` (line 465), then for each schedule performs a separate `findFirst` for an existing `status: 'running'` execution record (line 471) as a duplicate guard, then calls `executeSchedule`. Inside `executeSchedule` (line 501+), `next_run_at` is updated before execution, but this is a plain `update`, not a conditional compare-and-set. There is no transaction, advisory lock, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or unique constraint linking the fetch, the running-check, and the execution-record creation.

Two failure modes: (1) multi-instance — `config/index.ts:108` explicitly supports `PROCESS_ROLE = 'api' | 'worker' | 'gateway'`, and app.ts:220-225 starts the schedule processor in every process with role `worker` or `all`; two worker processes each fetch the same due rows and both pass the running-check before either has written a running record. (2) single-process overlap — `processSchedules` is an async function invoked by `setInterval` without an in-flight guard, so a tick whose DB round-trips exceed the 15s poll interval overlaps the next tick; JS concurrency allows both invocations to interleave at every `await`, hitting the same window. Impact is duplicate full workflow executions — duplicated outbound `api_call` actions, notifications, and state writes.
poc_description:
1. Enable a workflow schedule with a cron expression that is due immediately.
2. Introduce latency (e.g. many simultaneously-due schedules, or a second worker process via PROCESS_ROLE=worker) so two ticks process the same schedule concurrently.
3. Both ticks pass the running-execution check (findFirst at schedule.service.ts:471) before either has inserted a 'running' record, and both call executeSchedule.
4. Observe two schedule_execution_records and two full workflow executions with duplicated outbound action nodes for a single due trigger.
remediation_steps: Make the claim of a schedule atomic at the database level: update next_run_at with a conditional update (`WHERE id = ? AND next_run_at = :expectedNow`) and treat zero affected rows as "another worker claimed it", or wrap fetch-and-claim in a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (PostgreSQL), or use a unique partial index on (schedule_id) WHERE status='running' to reject the second execution. Also serialize ticks within a process by guarding processSchedules with an in-flight flag so a slow tick is not re-entered by the 15-second interval.
evidence: Static trace of the guard chain: `schedule.service.ts:465-485` — `findMany` (no lock) → `findFirst` running check (non-atomic) → `executeSchedule`; `schedule-processor.ts:31-35` — `setInterval(processSchedules, 15000)` with an async handler, so a slow tick overlaps the next; `config/index.ts:108,270` — `PROCESS_ROLE` enum `['all','api','worker','gateway']` documents multi-process worker deployments. No database transaction, advisory lock, or unique constraint guards the fetch-to-execution transition.
assumptions: Any enabled workflow schedule with side-effecting nodes; requires two overlapping scheduler ticks (high DB latency, many due schedules, or multi-worker deployment with PROCESS_ROLE=worker).
counterevidence: Mitigating controls found: the 15-second poll interval means overlap requires processing latency above 15s (atypical for small schedules); a pre-execution status update of next_run_at and last_run_at narrows the window; a skip on existing 'running' executions catches most replays; the provided infra deploys a single EC2 instance with a single systemd backend process, so the multi-instance variant of this race requires an operator-configured PROCESS_ROLE split that no shipped deployment script performs. However, none of these are atomic on the fetch-to-execute path, and the documented PROCESS_ROLE worker split makes concurrent processors a supported configuration, so the guard remains a check-then-act window rather than an enforcing control.
confidence_rationale: Static-only trace of the complete non-atomic guard chain; no database or running service available in this isolated assessment to execute a concurrent-tick PoC. Control flow, guard ordering, and absence of any atomicity mechanism (lock, unique constraint, or skipLocked) are fully verified from source.
severity_change_conditions: A dynamic demonstration of duplicate executions against a real database (e.g. instrumented concurrency test) would raise confidence and, if duplicates are trivially reproducible with default single-process timing, could raise severity to medium.

title: Archive symlink members dereferenced by fs.cp enable out-of-bounds file read into skill storage (zip/tar upload)
description: Symlink members inside an uploaded skill archive survive extraction (system `unzip -o` preserves symlinks) and are then dereferenced by `fs.cp` without `verbatimSymlinks` when the skill is copied to its permanent store and later into session workspaces, allowing an attacker to copy arbitrary out-of-archive files and directories into attacker-readable skill storage.
impact: Out-of-bounds file disclosure: any file or directory readable by the backend process user (e.g. `.env`, config files, `data/` contents including other tenants' skill stores, `~/.aws/credentials` if readable) is copied into the attacker's skill directory, where it is retrievable via skill download, workspace provisioning, or the skill listing. A directory symlink whose target is writable also creates a write pivot: extraction of a later archive (or the copy itself) can write through the symlink into the targeted directory. Integrity impact is limited (writes through a pre-planted writable directory symlink); no availability impact.
technical_analysis: `POST /api/skills/marketplace/upload-zip` writes the uploaded archive to a temp file and extracts it with the system command `unzip -o -q <zip> -d <extractDir>` (`src/services/skill-marketplace.service.ts:800`), with a `tar -xzf` fallback for tar archives (line 804). Unlike `..` path entries (which both tools refuse), Info-ZIP unzip and GNU tar both recreate symlink members as real symlinks in the extract directory. The service then discovers `SKILL.md` files and copies each skill directory to the permanent store with `cp(skillDir, permDir, { recursive: true })` (line 843) — Node's `fs/promises.cp` with default `verbatimSymlinks: false` dereferences symlinks, so a symlink member pointing at any readable path on the host causes the target file's contents (or, for directory symlinks, the whole subtree) to be copied into the attacker-controlled skill directory. The same unguarded pattern repeats at `src/services/workspace-manager.ts:1361` (`installSkillToWorkspace`, which copies from the skill store into every session workspace) and `:976` (`downloadSkill`), so the dereferenced content also lands in workspace trees and the S3 skill mirror. Related sibling sinks in the same flow: `workspace-manager.ts:1049-1057` extracts downloaded skill zips with `unzip -o` (or `python3 -m zipfile -e`, which also preserves/creates symlinks on unix) directly into the workspace. This is a distinct sink from the filed vuln-0013 (name-based path traversal write): here the skill name is irrelevant — the symlink itself performs the escape at copy time and yields primarily an out-of-bounds read.
poc_description:
1. Craft a zip containing a `SKILL.md` plus unix symlink members: one pointing at a secret file outside the archive (`myskill/leaked.txt -> /tmp/zip-poc/outside/secret.txt`) and one pointing at a directory (`myskill/outside-link -> /tmp/zip-poc/outside`). (In a real attack, target e.g. `/proc/self/environ` or the app's `.env`.)
2. Run the exact extraction command used by `installFromZip`: `unzip -o -q <zip> -d <extractDir>` — symlink members are preserved.
3. Run the exact copy used for the permanent store: Node `fs.cp(skillDir, permDir, {recursive:true})` with default options — the symlinks are dereferenced and out-of-archive content is copied into the skill store.
4. Read back the copied content from the skill store.
poc_script_code:
```bash
# /tmp/zip-poc — harmless local PoC replicating skill-marketplace.service.ts installFromZip flow
mkdir -p myskill outside && echo "secret-marker-for-poc" > outside/secret.txt
printf -- '---\nname: mys\ndescription: poc\n---\npoc\n' > myskill/SKILL.md
python3 - <<'PY'
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('malicious.zip','w') as z:
    z.writestr('myskill/SKILL.md', open('myskill/SKILL.md').read())
    for name, target in [('myskill/leaked.txt','/tmp/zip-poc/outside/secret.txt'),
                         ('myskill/outside-link','/tmp/zip-poc/outside')]:
        zi = zipfile.ZipInfo(name); zi.create_system = 3
        zi.external_attr = (0o120777 << 16)   # unix symlink
        z.writestr(zi, target)
PY
mkdir -p extractdir && unzip -o -q malicious.zip -d extractdir   # service's exact cmd
node -e "require('fs/promises').cp('extractdir/myskill','perm',{recursive:true}).then(()=>{  \
  const fs=require('fs'); \
  console.log(fs.readdirSync('perm')); \
  console.log('leaked:', fs.readFileSync('perm/leaked.txt','utf8')); })"
# -> [ 'SKILL.md', 'leaked.txt', 'outside-link' ]
# -> leaked: secret-marker-for-poc   (out-of-archive file content, dereferenced by fs.cp)
```
remediation_steps: Pass `verbatimSymlinks: true` to every `fs.cp` that copies extracted archive content (the permanent-store copy in `installFromZip`, and the workspace provisioning copies in `installSkillToWorkspace` and `downloadSkill`), then reject or strip any remaining symlinks in extracted skill directories. Preferably, reject any archive containing symlink or hardlink members at ingest time, mirroring the existing `..` entry protections, and validate post-extraction that no entry is a link before copying.
evidence: PoC executed in `/tmp/zip-poc` with the service's exact commands. (1) Hand-crafted zip containing unix symlink members `myskill/leaked.txt -> /tmp/zip-poc/outside/secret.txt` and `myskill/outside-link -> /tmp/zip-poc/outside`. (2) `unzip -o -q malicious.zip -d extractdir` — `ls -la extractdir/myskill` shows both symlinks preserved (`lrwxrwxrwx ... leaked.txt -> /tmp/zip-poc/outside/secret.txt`). (3) Node `fs.cp('extractdir/myskill','perm',{recursive:true})` (default `verbatimSymlinks:false`) — resulting `perm/leaked.txt` is a regular file containing the out-of-archive content `secret-marker-for-poc`, read back successfully.
assumptions: Authenticated org member with skill upload/install permissions (the upload-zip route requires only `authenticate`). The attacker's goal is exfiltration of readable backend files or planting writable directories.
counterevidence: Info-ZIP unzip and GNU tar both refuse `..` path members by default, so the classic zip-slip write via path traversal entries is blocked — this is the control that made the surface look safe. However, neither tool strips symlink members, and the subsequent `fs.cp` without `verbatimSymlinks` follows them (verified empirically), so the out-of-bounds read is confirmed reachable. Attack is limited to files readable by the backend process user; `unzip -o` overwrites existing extracted files only within the extract dir. This is a distinct sink from the filed vuln-0013 (arbitrary write via `../` in the skill name): here the write path stays inside the skill store; the defect is symlink following during copy, yielding a read primitive instead.
confidence_rationale: Local PoC executed with the exact extraction and copy commands the service uses (system `unzip -o -q`, Node `fs.cp(..., {recursive:true})` default flags), confirming both the symlink survival and the dereferencing copy; source trace verified for ingest, copy, and later workspace install.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating that a specific high-value secret (e.g. `.env` with auth secrets, or an S3/cloud credential readable by the backend user) is exfiltrable in a deployed configuration would raise this to high; a deployment where the backend user cannot read any sensitive files would lower it to medium.
